On Design Principles for Private Adaptive Optimizers

Arun Ganesh ††thanks: Google Research, {arunganesh, mcmahan}@google.com    Brendan McMahan11footnotemark: 1    Abhradeep Thakurta ††thanks: Google DeepMind, athakurta@google.com
Abstract

The spherical noise added to gradients in differentially private (DP) training undermines the performance of adaptive optimizers like AdaGrad and Adam, and hence many recent works have proposed algorithms to address this challenge. However, the empirical results in these works focus on simple tasks and models and the conclusions may not generalize to model training in practice. In this paper we survey several of these variants, and develop better theoretical intuition for them as well as perform empirical studies comparing them. We find that a common intuition of aiming for unbiased estimates of second moments of gradients in adaptive optimizers is misguided, and instead that a simple technique called scale-then-privatize (which does not achieve unbiased second moments) has more desirable theoretical behaviors and outperforms all other variants we study on a small-scale language model training task. We additionally argue that scale-then-privatize causes the noise addition to better match the application of correlated noise mechanisms which are more desirable to use in practice.

1 Introduction

Language models often have sparse gradients in training, and it is now well-understood that using adaptive optimizers leads to better training performance for these models [25]. At a high level, adaptive optimizers maintain 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, an estimate of the average coordinate-wise square of the gradients, and rather than use a constant learning rate, use a per-coordinate learning proportional to 1/𝝂1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}} (where 𝝂\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}} denotes the per-coordinate square root; the application of per-coordinate learning rate is also commonly called preconditioning). Intuitively, 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} represents the information learned about the geometry of the gradients seen so far, and the use of per-coordinate learning rates is an attempt to adapt the gradients to this geometry.

When training a model with differential privacy (DP) [11] and a non-adaptive optimizer, usually noise is added to the gradients and then the noisy gradients are passed to the non-adaptive optimizer in a black-box manner. One can analogously train with DP using an adaptive optimizer in a black-box manner, but doing so indirectly noises 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}. Roughly speaking, this noise causes the coordinates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} to be more similar in magnitude, i.e. impedes the ability of the adaptive optimizer to learn the geometry of the gradients and makes it behave more similarly to a non-adaptive optimizer. Consequently, even for tasks where non-private adaptive optimizers outperform non-adaptive optimizers, for DP adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers may achieve similar performance [23]. In turn, many recent works (e.g., [2, 15, 16, 23, 13]) have proposed new variants of private adaptive optimizers that aim to recover the benefits of adaptive optimizers by restoring the ability of the adaptive optimizer to learn the geometry in the presence of noise.

In spite of the many proposed variants, our understanding of these variants remains limited in a few aspects. First, the empirical evaluation in many of these papers is restricted to tasks such as CIFAR or text classification tasks such as SNLI/QNLI, which are much simpler than the token prediction tasks language models are trained to solve in practice. Hence it is not clear if the conclusions of existing empirical studies extend to production-scale fine-tuning of language models with DP. Second, with the exception of [13], most work only focuses on adding independent noise in different iterations, but it is often preferable in practice to use noise that is instead correlated across iterations [20]. Even [13] focuses primarily on the role of correlated noise in the estimation of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, and less on the interplay between correlated noise and changing per-coordinate learning rates in Adam.

1.1 Our Contributions

We survey several private variants of adaptive optimizers, detailed in Section 3. We analyze these variants both by studying their theoretical underpinnings, and by conducting experiments comparing their effectiveness for training a Transformer language model (TinyBERT) on a token prediction task.

Theoretical contributions (Section 4): We build theoretical intuition about the interplay between noise addition and adaptive optimizers. We propose several insights on how to design private adaptive optimizers and give quantitative justification for each. Our main insights are:

  • •

    Unbiased ν\boldsymbol{\nu} is not necessary: Combining DP gradients and adaptive optimizers in a black-box fashion gives biased estimates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, and previous works have suggested improving private adaptive optimizers by using an unbiased estimate instead. We argue that this is somewhat misguided, as these approaches do not distinguish variance in the data from variance due to DP noise. We further argue that a previously proposed technique which we call scale-then-privatize, which uses 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} to clip and noise the gradients in a non-isotropic manner, is better because it both learns the non-private geometry and causes the noisy gradient distribution to match this geometry.

  • •

    Two regimes for unbiased ν\boldsymbol{\nu}: We further argue that using 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} which is an unbiased estimate of 𝝂∗\boldsymbol{\nu}^{*}, the value of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} we’d arrive at with the same gradients and no noise, can be harmful in certain parameter regimes. When using unbiased but noisy estimates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, we show that if the dimension is sufficiently large (as a function of the noise level and batch size), a constant fraction of the coordinates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} (which is estimating a weighted average of squared values, i.e. non-negative values), will be negative. While this can be corrected by e.g. taking only the positive part of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, even with these corrections this can lead to undesirable learning behaviors. This observation can explain a disparity between empirical results in the literature operating with lower-dimensional tasks and our empirical results on transformer training.

  • •

    Scale-then-privatize benefits correlated noise: We lastly consider the interplay between correlated noise in private optimizers and adaptive optimizers. Correlated noise, also known as DP-MF, attempts to cancel out the noise added in one iteration in subsequent iterations, to reduce the total amount of noise added across the learning process. However, when using an adaptive optimizer the per-coordinate learning rate changes across iterations, which may impede this cancellation. We show that scale-then-privatize causes the effective noise added to each update (rather than each gradient, i.e. the noise after rescaling by the per-coordinate learning rates) to be roughly isotropic, suggesting that noise cancellation should be about as effective as in the non-adaptive setting, regardless of changes in the per-coordinate learning rate over time.

Empirical results (Section 5): We conduct experiments where we train models using the different variants consider. We first observe that in a one-dimensional setting, a technique called independent moment estimation significantly outperforms the baseline of using adaptive optimizers in a black-box manner. However, when we move to a token prediction task where we train TinyBERT, a transformer model with only a few million trainable parameters, most variants we consider do worse than the black-box approach. This supports our theoretical intuition that approaches targeting unbiased estimates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} can break down once the dimension is sufficiently high, and furthermore that this occurs at model sizes much smaller than those used in production settings. We also demonstrate that unlike the other variants, scale-then-privatize outperforms the black-box approach for this task. In conjunction with our theoretical intuition, our empirical results suggest that the empirical results in past works may not generalize even to small-scale token prediction tasks that better resemble model training in production settings, and the principles used to design private adaptive optimizers in past work may need to be reconsidered.

Then, Gt={𝐠1,j∣j∈[B]}G_{t}=\{\mathbf{g}_{1,j}\mid j\in[B]\} represents the set of BB gradients for round tt. We define the clipping operator

𝐠t=1B​∑𝐠t,j∈Gt𝐠t,jor𝐠t=1B​∑𝐠t,j∈Gtclip⁡(𝐠t,j;ζ)\mathbf{g}_{t}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{\mathbf{g}_{t,j}\in G_{t}}\mathbf{g}_{t,j}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathbf{g}_{t}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{\mathbf{g}_{t,j}\in G_{t}}\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\mathbf{g}_{t,j};\zeta\right)

for non-private vs private algorithms respectively.

2.1 Private training via DP-SGD and DP-MF

An algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is (ε,δCLOSE(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP if given two datasets D,D′D,D^{\prime} that are adjacent according to some adjacency definition, and any set of possible outputs SS we have:

𝐏𝐫[A(D)∈S]≤eε𝐏𝐫[A(D′)∈S]+δ.\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[A(D)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\mathop{\mathbf{Pr}}[A(D^{\prime})\in S]+\delta.

We focus on the zero-out adjacency as defined in [21]: D,D′D,D^{\prime} are adjacent if D′D^{\prime} is equal to DD (or vice-versa) except one example is replaced with a placeholder ⊥\bot, whose gradient is zero everywhere.11 1 For production uses where one user may contribute multiple examples, our results extend naturally to user-level DP, see for example [5]. A standard DP for answering a vector-valued query on a dataset is the Gaussian mechanism: If ff is a query such that for any adjacent D,D′D,D^{\prime} we have ‖f⁡(D)−f⁡(D′)‖2≤Δ\left\|f(D)-f(D^{\prime})\right\|_{2}\leq\Delta, the Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier σ\sigma answers ff by returning f⁡(D)+𝐳f(D)+\mathbf{z}, where 𝐳∼N⁡(𝟎,σ2​Δ2​𝕀)\mathbf{z}\sim N(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\Delta^{2}\mathbb{I}).

DP-SGD [22, 4, 1] is a canonical private learning algorithm which satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP. In DP-SGD, given in Algorithm 1, in each round tt we sample a batch of examples from the dataset DD and compute their gradients GtG_{t} on the current model, clip the gradients to have bounded ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, and add independent Gaussian noise to their average. We then use this as a noisy gradient in SGD, or another first-order method such as Adam, as the standard privacy guarantees of DP-SGD do not depend on the first-order method by the post-processing property of DP.

DP-MF [12], or equivalently, DP-SGD with correlated noise, is also given in Algorithm 1. In this variant of DP-SGD the noise used in different rounds is correlated, so that some of the noise added in one round is cancelled out in subsequent rounds. The amount of cancellation is specified by a lower triangular noise correlating matrix22 2 We use 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} for consistency with other works; the matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C} is called the strategy matrix, and plays an important role in the privacy analysis of DP-MF, but will not be critical to our work. 𝐂−1∈ℝT×T{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}, which produces noise (𝐂−1​𝐳)t=∑j=1t𝐂−1t,j​𝐳j({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}_{t,j}\mathbf{z}_{j} in round tt. The case 𝐂−1=𝐈{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}=\mathbf{I} retrieves the independent noise of DP-SGD. Typically, 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} is chosen via a suitable matrix factorization, e.g. [8, 6]. Typically the main diagonal of 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} will be positive (often 1), with negative values below the main diagonal. For example,

𝐂−1=[100−0.5100−0.51]{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ -0.5&1&0\\ 0&-0.5&1\end{bmatrix}

adds one unit of noise on each round, and then subtracts off half of this noise on the subsequent iteration (while also adding one unit of new IID noise).

The privacy guarantees of the Gaussian mechanism as well as the privacy analysis of DP-SGD and DP-MF via privacy analysis of the Gaussian mechanism are by now well-understood. For the most part precise privacy guarantees and parameters are immaterial to the discussions in this paper, and we will focus on analyzing DP-Adam with a fixed noise multiplier agnostic of the corresponding privacy parameters.

2.2 Background on AdaGrad/Adam

While there are a number of adaptive optimizers of interest, for simplicity we will primarily focus on Adam (of [14]), and occasionally also consider AdaGrad (of [19, 10, 18]); many of our theoretical observations and experimental conclusions should readily transfer to other adaptive optimizers. Pseudocode for both algorithms is given in Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3.

The key idea of both is to maintain 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, a (weighted) sum of all squared gradients 𝐠2\mathbf{g}^{2} seen so far, and use (roughly) 1/𝝂1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}} as a vector of per-coordinate learning rates. While ideally for mm-dimensional gradients we would maintain a m×mm\times m matrix estimating 𝔼𝐠​[𝐠𝐠⊤]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{g}}[\mathbf{g}\mathbf{g}^{\top}], due to memory limitations in practice it is more common to maintain an estimate of 𝔼𝐠​[𝐠2]\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{g}}[\mathbf{g}^{2}]. We hence give the pseudocode for the latter throughout.

AdaGrad chooses 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} to be exactly the sum of squared gradients. Intuitively, this retrieves the standard theoretical choice of learning rate decay 1/t1/\sqrt{t} for SGD in the one-dimensional setting if the gradient is always a constant, and then maintains this behavior even if we insert any number of zero gradients to the input stream, or scale all the gradients by a constant. Adam uses a sum of decaying squared gradients, and normalizes the sum to get 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} before computing the per-coordinate learning rates using 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} instead of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}. Intuitively, Adam recovers AdaGrad’s behavior of using larger learning rate in coordinates that have been updated less, but (i) the decay enables it to adapt to changes in the magnitudes throughout the optimization process, whereas AdaGrad may be stuck using smaller learning rates in coordinates that have previously seen many large gradients, and (ii) the normalization means it retrieves behavior closer to constant learning rates rather than decaying learning rates, which may be preferable in practice.

2.2.1 Square-Then-Average

As written, AdaGrad and Adam first average the gradients in a batch before squaring. One could alternatively square the individual gradients before averaging. If we view the choice of 1/𝝂1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}} as trying to retrieve the 1/M1/\sqrt{M} learning rate that is standard for MM-smooth losses, one could argue that the variance of gradients is a proxy for this squared smoothness, and the average squared gradient is a better estimate for the variance than the squared average gradient. While exploring the benefits of “square-then-average” rather than “average-then-square” is an interesting direction, we focus on average-then-square for two reasons. First, average-then-square is the variant used by the original Adam paper [14] and the one commonly used in practice, so by focusing on this variant our results are more directly applicable to Adam’s use in practice. Second, the decision to use square-then-average rather than average-then-square is relevant even for non-private learning, and hence somewhat outside the scope of this paper.

3 Survey of DP-Adam Variants

Here we define and discuss some proposed DP variants of Adam. It is usually straightforward to define the analogous versions of these algorithms for other adaptive optimizers such as AdaGrad. For simplicity we present the algorithms using independent noise (DP-SGD), but they can be analogously defined using DP-MF in all cases by letting 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} be the ttth value of correlated noise, i.e. using (𝐂−1​𝐳)t({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{t} instead of 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} as in Algorithm 1.

We first give pseudocode in Fig. 1 for all the variants and then discuss them in more detail in the following subsections. Algorithm 4 restates the non-private Adam algorithm for convenience, Algorithm 5 gives DP-Adam via post-processing with the differences from Adam highlighted in blue, and then in the remaining private variants of Adam we highlight the differences with DP-Adam via post-processing rather than non-private Adam.

3.1 Post-Processing (“Standard” DP-Adam)

Arguably the simplest and most common way to make Adam private is post-processing (Algorithm 5): privatize the computation of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t}, and then use the privatized 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} in Adam in a black-box manner.

The main issue with the algorithm is that while the Gaussian noise is mean-zero and hence 𝝁t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t} is unbiased, 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} is biased. In particular, if 𝝂t∗\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}^{*} is the value of 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} one would get from the unnoised Algorithm 2 for the same gradient stream33 3 Note that this is not the same as the value of 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} one would arrive at with non-private Adam, because non-private Adam would take a different trajectory and hence receive a different gradient stream., then we can compute the bias for each term as follows. For 𝝂1\boldsymbol{\nu}_{1} we have:

𝔼⁡[𝝂1]=(1−β2)​𝔼​[𝐠~12]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\nu}_{1}]=(1-\beta_{2})\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{\mathbf{g}}_{1}^{2}] =(1−β2)​(𝐠t2+ζ2B2​𝔼​[𝐳t2])\displaystyle=(1-\beta_{2})(\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}+\frac{\zeta^{2}}{B^{2}}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_{t}^{2}])

Now by induction assume 𝔼⁡[𝝂t−1]=𝝂t−1∗+(1−β2t−1)​ζ2​σ2B2\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t-1}]=\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t-1}^{*}+(1-\beta_{2}^{t-1})\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}. Then:

=β2​𝝂t−1∗+β2​(1−β2t−1)​ζ2​σ2B2+(1−β2)​(𝐠t2+ζ2​σ2B2)\displaystyle=\beta_{2}\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t-1}^{*}+\beta_{2}(1-\beta_{2}^{t-1})\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+(1-\beta_{2})(\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}+\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}})

Hence by induction, each 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} has bias (1−β2t)​ζ2​σ2B2⋅𝟏(1-\beta_{2}^{t})\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}\cdot\boldsymbol{1}, i.e. 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} has bias ζ2​σ2B2⋅𝟏\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}\cdot\boldsymbol{1}. For DP-MF a slightly more nuanced calculation is involved, which we give in Appendix A.

The effect of this bias effectively causes all coordinates where 𝝂t∗\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}^{*} is sufficiently small, i.e. where gradients have small magnitude or have non-zero mass infrequently, to use a much smaller per-coordinate learning rate 1/𝝂t1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}}. Tang et al. [23] argue that this makes Adam resemble DP-SGD with momentum, since Adam with 𝝂t∝𝟏\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}\propto\boldsymbol{1} retrieves SGD with momentum and the noise causes 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}’s coordinates to be more uniform.

3.2 Independent Moment Estimation

One way to fix the bias in 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} is independent moment estimation (Algorithm 6), as defined in [13]: we separately noise 𝝁t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t} and 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}. Equivalently, we treat (𝐠t,c​𝐠t2)(\mathbf{g}_{t},c\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}) for c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}^{+} as a 2​m2m-dimensional vector to be noised in each round. Independent moment estimation adds i.i.d Gaussian noise to this vector, and then uses the first mm coordinates to update 𝝁t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t} in Adam and the second mm coordinates to update 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}. Here, cc is a scaling term that trades off which of 𝝁t,𝝂t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t},\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} we want to add more noise to: When cc is high the ℓ2\ell_{2}-sensitivity of this vector is proportional to cc, so 𝝁t\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t} is over-noised. When cc is low the sensitivity is ≈ζ\approx\zeta, but 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} is scaled by cc so it is over-noised.

For simplicity we consider independent moment estimation with c=1c=1. Under the zero-out adjacency, the sensitivity of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} remains ζ/B\zeta/B, and the sensitivity of 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} is bounded as:

This sensitivity bound is tight in the case where all 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} are the same. By composition (which states that the combination of two Gaussian mechanisms with noise multipliers 2​σ\sqrt{2}\sigma satisfiy the privacy guarantees of one Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier σ\sigma), to achieve the same privacy as e.g. DP-Adam via post-processing, it then suffices to add noise with standard deviation 2​ζB\frac{\sqrt{2}\zeta}{B} to 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} and standard deviation 2​(2​B+1)​ζ2B2\frac{\sqrt{2}(2B+1)\zeta^{2}}{B^{2}} to 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} and this is tight again in the case where all 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} are the same. Hence we arrive at the variant of Adam defined in Algorithm 6.

[13] observed that under the replace adjacency44 4 In the replace adjacency DD and D′D^{\prime} are adjacent if we can replace an example in DD with any other example (not necessarily the special example ⊥\bot used in the zero-out adjacency) to get D′D^{\prime}., the sensitivity of the vector (𝐠t,c​𝐠t2)(\mathbf{g}_{t},c\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}) could be the same as the sensitivity of the vector 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} for cc as large as 1/2​ζ21/2\zeta^{2}. The intuitive reason there is no increase in sensitivity is when bounding the sensitivity of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t}, the “worst-case” pair of values 𝐠t,𝐠t′\mathbf{g}_{t},\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\prime} a gradient takes on for two adjacent datasets satisfies 𝐠t=−𝐠t′\mathbf{g}_{t}=-\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\prime}. But in this case, 𝐠t2=𝐠t′2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}=\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\prime 2}, i.e. concatenating c​𝐠t2c\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} doesn’t increase the sensitivity. Furthermore, if c≤1/2​ζ2c\leq 1/2\zeta^{2}, [13] shows that 𝐠t=−𝐠t′\mathbf{g}_{t}=-\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\prime} remains the worst-case for the sensitivity of the pair (𝐠t,c​𝐠t2)(\mathbf{g}_{t},c\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2})55 5 This bound on cc is for the case where m>1m>1 and we use DP-SGD. If the dimension is m=1m=1 they show an improved bound. Furthermore, if using DP-MF instead of DP-SGD for noise addition, the bound also depends on the choice of factorization.. However, for the zero-out adjacency we focus on the worst case is 𝐠t=𝟎\mathbf{g}_{t}=\boldsymbol{0} instead of 𝐠t=−𝐠t′\mathbf{g}_{t}=-\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\prime}, i.e. in the zero-out adjacency strictly more noise is required if additionally noising 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}.

Unlike post-processing, the noisy second moment estimate 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} is not necessarily positive because the noise 𝐳t,2\mathbf{z}_{t,2} added to it is not squared. Hence we need to take the positive part of 𝝂t\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t} before taking the square root. There are other ways to correct this to avoid taking the square root of a negative number, for example by using max⁡{𝝂t,εs2}\sqrt{\max\{\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t},\varepsilon_{s}^{2}\}} instead of max⁡{𝝂t,𝟎}+εs⋅𝟙\sqrt{\max\{\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t},\boldsymbol{0}\}}+\varepsilon_{s}\cdot\mathbb{1}. We do not believe the behaviors of these variants substantially differ, as they are never more than a constant factor apart from each other.

3.3 Bias Correction

Bias correction (Algorithm 7), proposed by Tang et al. [23], handles the bias in 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} by directly subtracting the bias ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}} from it.

As with independent moment estimation, bias correction gives an estimate of the second moment 𝝂^t−ζ2​σ2B2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}-\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}} that is unbiased, but can be negative, and hence we need to take the positive part of it before taking its square root to compute the per-coordinate learning rates.

3.4 Scale-Then-Privatize

All approaches we have discussed so far clip gradients in the standard ℓ2\ell_{2} norm. However, 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} defines a different norm/geometry, such that Adam taking a gradient step using different per-coordinate learning rates η/𝝂^t\eta/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}} in the “standard” geometry is equivalent to taking a gradient step using constant learning rate η\eta in this geometry. We could instead consider clipping and noising gradients in this geometry, which we refer to as scale-then-privatize (Algorithm 8). Ideally we would use 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}, which contains the most “up-to-date” estimate of the geometry, to scale each 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j}, but this of course introduces a circular dependence between the parameters. We instead use 𝝂^t−1\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1} to scale 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j}. For small values of tt, 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} and 𝝂^t−1\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1} may differ largely, but as tt increases 𝝂^t−1\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1} will become a reasonably good estimate of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}.

Here, 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} is the scaling/geometry we use for clipping and noising. In Line 4, rather than clip 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} we clip 𝐬t⊙𝐠t,j\mathbf{s}_{t}\odot\mathbf{g}_{t,j}. In Line 6 we noise the scaled gradient, and then undo the scaling by 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} to return the clipped gradients to the original geometry before passing it to the Adam black-box. Since we are adding isotropic noise to the clipped objects, this has the same DP guarantees as Algorithm 5. An equivalent view is that we are clipping 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} to a non-isotropic ellipsoid defined by 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} and adding noise in the shape of this ellipsoid, where when 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} is constant across coordinates, this ellipsoid is a sphere. Li et al. [15], Li et al. [16] argued for scale-then-privatize (referring to it as clipping the preconditioned gradients) because it avoids adding excess noise in coordinates where the scaling 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} is small.

Connection to delayed preconditioners: Scale-then-privatize is an extreme instantiation of the idea of delayed preconditioners of [16]. Delayed preconditioners is a technique where in each set of s1+s2s_{1}+s_{2} iterations we (i) do s1s_{1} iterations of doing no scaling of gradients and accumulating the average of the corresponding s1s_{1} batches of gradients (ii) after s1s_{1} iterations, use the gradient accumulated over those iterations to update ν^\hat{\nu}, and then (iii) do s2s_{2} iterations where we use ν^\hat{\nu} to scale the gradients (ν^\hat{\nu} is not updated in these iterations). Scale-then-privatize is equivalent to setting s1=0,s2=1s_{1}=0,s_{2}=1. We do not extensively study delayed preconditioners separately from scale-then-privatize as (i) the use of both un-preconditioned and preconditioned gradients, as well as the reduced frequency of updates to ν^\hat{\nu}, are cumbersome to include in our theoretical studies and (ii) the added hyperparameters s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} need to be separately tuned which greatly increases the time needed to run experiments using delayed preconditioners.

3.4.1 Noising the Update

Another private variant of DP-Adam one could consider is to add isotropic noise to the updates 𝝁^/𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}} directly rather than to the gradients. For simplicity lets consider Adam with no momentum in the first moment (i.e., setting β1=0\beta_{1}=0) and εs=0\varepsilon_{s}=0. Now our goal is simply to noise the individual updates 𝐠t/𝝂^t\mathbf{g}_{t}/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}}. The main issue with this approach is that the worst-case sensitivity of the updates can be quite poor. Consider the one-dimensional setting, when the gradient of the first t−1t-1 batches is 0, and the tt-th batch GtG_{t} has a single example with a non-zero gradient 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j}. Then, we will have 𝝂^t=1−β21−β2t​𝐠t2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}=\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}, so 𝐠t/𝝂^t=sign⁡(𝐠t,j)⋅1−β2t1−β2\mathbf{g}_{t}/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}}=\sign(\mathbf{g}_{t,j})\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}{1-\beta_{2}}}. For β2≈0.999\beta_{2}\approx 0.999 this could be as large as ≈30\approx 30 for sufficiently large tt, and furthermore it is not a function of the batch size, i.e. the sensitivity of the updates cannot be made to vanish by increasing the batch size. Even worse, this is only the sensitivity analysis when considering a single update. In reality, the gradient 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} will affect the value of 𝝂^t+1,𝝂^t+2,…\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t+1},\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t+2},\ldots, and hence indirectly affect the magnitude of all updates from tt to TT, so the actual sensitivity of the sequence of all updates with respect to 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} could be much larger than the sensitivity of just the tt-th update. In short, noising the updates requires too much noise to be practical unless we can arrive at a far more refined sensitivity analysis.

However, from the idea of noising the update we can arrive at scale-then-privatize; if we had 𝝂^t−1=𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}, for β1=0\beta_{1}=0 one can see that scale-then-privatize actually does add isotropic noise to the update (this is an idea we will revisit in Section 4.5). Hence, one intuition for scale-then-privatize is that as long as 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} does not change too much in any single iteration, scale-then-privatize approximately retrieves the idea of noising the updates, but with a far smaller amount of noise required.

3.5 Preconditioner from Side Information

Finally, as a baseline one could consider computing a preconditioner 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} prior to training or during training using some auxiliary data, e.g. in-distribution public data, and then use this value rather than the noisy 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} to choose per-coordinate learning rates. Asi et al. [3], Li et al. [15] proposed the online version assuming some side information. In practice sources of side information such as in-distribution public data are not readily available [24], hence this method largely serves as a baseline rather than a practical method of interest in our setting.

4 Theoretical Explorations

In this section, we make a number of claims about the different variants of Adam discussed in Section 3, for each trying to give some theoretical justification. At the end of each section we summarize the main takeaway in a highlighted text box, for readers who are interested in the claims moreso than the theoretical justifications for them.

4.1 A Quadratic Example

To better understand the impact of noise on DP-Adam and its variants, we introduce the following running example we will reference throughout the section: Consider a two-dimensional quadratic loss where the loss of model (x,y)(x,y) on example (a,b)(a,b) is cx2​(x−a)2+cy2​(y−b)2\frac{c_{x}}{2}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{c_{y}}{2}(y-b)^{2}. We assume the examples (a,b)(a,b) come from the distribution N⁡(𝟎,𝕀)N(\boldsymbol{0},\mathbb{I}), and in each iteration we sample a new example from this distribution and use its gradient in the first-order optimizer.

If we start optimization with x,y≈0x,y\approx 0, for most gradients (gx,gy)(g_{x},g_{y}) we sample we will have |gx||g_{x}| is within a constant factor of cxc_{x}, and |gy||g_{y}| is within a constant factor of cyc_{y}. For (non-private) Adam, this means we will have 𝝂≈(cx2,cy2)\boldsymbol{\nu}\approx(c_{x}^{2},c_{y}^{2}) and hence Adam would use per-coordinate learning rates ≈(1/cx,1/cy)\approx(1/c_{x},1/c_{y}). For this axis-aligned loss, this approximately retrieves using the inverse of the Hessian as a scaling on the gradient, i.e. the updates used in Newton’s method. In settings where cx≫cyc_{x}\gg c_{y} or cx≪cyc_{x}\ll c_{y}, this will lead to much faster convergence than using the same learning rate for both coordinates.

What happens if we use DP-Adam (via post-processing) instead? For now, let us ignore clipping and just consider Adam with a noise (zx,zy)∼N⁡(𝟎,σ2​𝕀)(z_{x},z_{y})\sim N(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}\mathbb{I}) added to each gradient. The expected per-coordinate square of the gradient in each iteration is now (cx2+σ2,cy2+σ2)(c_{x}^{2}+\sigma^{2},c_{y}^{2}+\sigma^{2}). In turn, if σ≫cx\sigma\gg c_{x} or σ≫cy\sigma\gg c_{y}, we are going to use a smaller per-coordinate learning rate ≈1/σ\approx 1/\sigma in the corresponding coordinate. Put another way, one intuition for DP-Adam is that the noise imposes a floor of 1/σ1/\sigma on the per-coordinate learning rates, which prevents DP-Adam from distinguishing between coordinates where the “correct” per-coordinate learning rate is smaller than 1/σ1/\sigma.

4.2 Variance from Privacy vs. Variance from Data

A seemingly key advantage of independent moment estimation (Algorithm 6) and bias correction (Algorithm 7) is that the second moment estimate 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} is unbiased. However, using the quadratic example from Section 4.1, we argue that this is not the right goal for designing private adaptive optimizers.

Let’s consider the following “noiseless preconditioner” variant of DP-Adam: We use the noisy gradients to compute 𝝁\boldsymbol{\mu}, but compute 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} using noiseless gradients. This is effectively Algorithm 6 or Algorithm 7 if they could achieve an even stronger goal of computing 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} exactly, rather than just exactly in expectation. Is this algorithm necessarily preferable over DP-Adam via post-processing? While this algorithm uses the right learning rates (1/cx,1/cy)(1/c_{x},1/c_{y}) for the non-private distribution of gradients, for the private distribution of gradients these are not necessarily the right learning rates. One way to see this: Consider the (non-private) gradient distribution if instead of drawing the samples from N⁡(0,𝕀)N(0,\mathbb{I}) we draw the samples (a,b)(a,b) from

N⁡(𝟎,[cx2+σ2cx200cy2+σ2cy2]).N\left(\boldsymbol{0},\begin{bmatrix}\frac{c_{x}^{2}+\sigma^{2}}{c_{x}^{2}}&0\\ 0&\frac{c_{y}^{2}+\sigma^{2}}{c_{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\right).

The gradient distribution for this data distribution is the same as the gradient distribution we get from original data distribution of N⁡(𝟎,𝕀)N(\boldsymbol{0},\mathbb{I}) if we additionally add noise for privacy N⁡(0,σ2​𝕀)N(0,\sigma^{2}\mathbb{I}) added to the gradients. However, for this gradient distribution non-private Adam will not try to learn the preconditioner (cx2,cy2)(c_{x}^{2},c_{y}^{2}) which Algorithm 6 and Algorithm 7 are trying to learn, but the preconditioner which is learned by DP-Adam via post-processing (Algorithm 5). This means one of two things is true: Either (i) “noiseless preconditioner” DP-Adam (and algorithms like Algorithm 6 and Algorithm 7 which are trying to emulate it) is not the right algorithm to mimic: there are two learning problems which have the same gradient distributions, i.e. are fundamentally the same learning problem, but for which noiseless preconditioner DP-Adam leads to wildly different optimization behaviors.

4.3 Benefits of Scale-Then-Privatize

We argue that, at least in idealized settings, scale-then-privatize simultaneously: (i) adequately matches its preconditioner to the geometry of the non-private gradients (ii) matches the geometry of the non-private gradients and private gradients, such that property (i) is desirable even in light of the previous section.

4.3.1 Scale-Then-Privatize Roughly Retrieves the Non-Private Geometry

Our first claim in this section is that, at least in idealized settings, scale-then-privatize arrives at a preconditioner roughly proportional to the preconditioner we’d arrive at non-privately, which by rescaling the learning rate allows us to retrieve some of the benefits of non-private adaptive optimizers.

We will study the setting where 𝐠t=𝐠\mathbf{g}_{t}=\mathbf{g} in all rounds (and hence 𝝂^t∗=𝐠2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*}=\mathbf{g}^{2} in all rounds) and εs\varepsilon_{s} is negligible and can be treated as zero. While this is a very simple setting, (i) as demonstrated in the previous section, other approaches proposed in the literature fail in simple settings, so it is worth validating that an approach works in such settings and (ii) we believe this setting still gives good intuition for the desirable behaviors of scale-then-privatize.

For ease of presentation, we fix ζ=1,β2=0.999\zeta=1,\beta_{2}=0.999, the latter being a standard choice for Adam. We will also focus on the later iterations of training where tt is large, such that we can use the approximation β2t≈0\beta_{2}^{t}\approx 0. We give the same analysis in more generality in Appendix B.

Using these settings and approximations, we start by rewriting 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} in Algorithm 8 as:

𝝂^t\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} =𝝂t=0.999⋅𝝂t−1+0.001⋅𝐠~t2=\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}=0.999\cdot\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t-1}+0.001\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t}^{2}=
=0.999⋅𝝂^t−1+0.001​(𝐠t+1B​(𝐳t/𝐬t))2=0.999⋅𝝂^t−1+0.001​(𝐠t+1B​(𝐳t⊙(𝝂^t−1+εs)))2\displaystyle=0.999\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+0.001\left(\mathbf{g}_{t}+\frac{1}{B}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}/\mathbf{s}_{t}\right)\right)^{2}=0.999\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+0.001\left(\mathbf{g}_{t}+\frac{1}{B}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t}\odot\left(\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}}+\varepsilon_{s}\right)\right)\right)^{2} (1)

Taking expectation over 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} (conditioned on all randomness before iteration tt):

𝔼⁡[𝝂^t]=0.999⋅𝝂^t−1+0.001​(𝐠2+σ2B2​𝝂^t−1)=(0.999+0.001⋅σ2B2)​𝝂^t−1+0.001⋅𝐠2.\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}]=0.999\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+0.001\left(\mathbf{g}^{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}\right)=\left(0.999+0.001\cdot\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}\right)\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+0.001\cdot\mathbf{g}^{2}.

𝝂^t−1=11−σ2B2​𝐠2=11−σ2B2​(𝝂^t−1∗)2,\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}}\mathbf{g}^{2}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}^{*})^{2},

then 𝔼⁡[𝝂^t]=𝝂^t−1\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}]=\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}, i.e. 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} does not change in expectation. In other words, assuming σ/B<1\sigma/B<1, a “steady state” for 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} (in expectation) is proportional to 𝝂^∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*} as desired. Furthermore, in coordinates where 𝝂^t−1>11−σ2B2​𝐠2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}>\frac{1}{1-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}}\mathbf{g}^{2}, 𝔼⁡[𝝂^t]<𝝂^t−1\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}]<\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1} and similarly in coordinates where 𝝂^t−1<11−σ2B2​𝐠2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}<\frac{1}{1-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}}\mathbf{g}^{2}, 𝔼⁡[𝝂^t]<𝝂^t−1\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}]<\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}, i.e. 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} converges towards its steady state. 4.3.2 Scale-Then-Privatize Aligns the Private and Non-Private Geometry

We now return to the quadratic example of Section 4.1 and see how scale-then-privatize affects the behavior in contrast with noiseless preconditioner DP-Adam. Per the previous section, we expect that the preconditioner used by DP-Adam with scale-then-privatize (Algorithm 8) is roughly proportional to (1/cx,1/cy)(1/c_{x},1/c_{y}). If we assume the preconditioner is equal to α⋅(1/cx,1/cy)\alpha\cdot(1/c_{x},1/c_{y}), the distribution of the noise added to gradients is (cx/α,cy/α)⊙(zx,zy)(c_{x}/\alpha,c_{y}/\alpha)\odot(z_{x},z_{y}), zx,zy∼N⁡(0,1)z_{x},z_{y}\sim N(0,1). So the overall distribution of the gradients when x=0,y=0x=0,y=0 is

N⁡(𝟎,(1+α2)​[cx200cy2]).N\left(\boldsymbol{0},(1+\alpha^{2})\begin{bmatrix}c_{x}^{2}&0\\ 0&c_{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right).

Hence the preconditioner α⋅(1/cx,1/cy)\alpha\cdot(1/c_{x},1/c_{y}) actually matches the geometry of the gradients, up to a proportionality of α21+α2\frac{\alpha^{2}}{1+\alpha^{2}} (which can be corrected for with an appropriate choice of learning rate). This example demonstrates that when DP-Adam with scale-then-privatize retrieves the noiseless preconditioner (up to some proportionality), it also retrieves the right second moments of the public distribution of gradients (up to some other proportionality). This is in contrast with DP-Adam via post-processing which matches the private preconditioner with the private gradient distribution but doesn’t match the noiseless preconditioner even up to proportionality, or noiseless preconditioner DP-Adam which exactly uses the noiseless preconditioner but whose gradient distribution is a mismatch with this preconditioner.

4.4 Potentially Negative Estimates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}

Our next claim is that there are two regimes for techniques which use unbiased estimates of 𝝂^t∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*}, depending on the ratio RR of the average coordinate of 𝝂^t∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*} to the noise multiplier σ\sigma. As previously discussed, techniques such as bias correction and independent moment estimation which estimate 𝝂^t∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*} in an unbiased manner can potentially underestimate 𝝂^t∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*}, and even produce negative estimates. We first attempt to quantify when this is a concern, and then explain the potential adverse effects of having negative coordinates in 𝝂^∗\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*}.

4.4.1 Regimes for Unbiased Estimators of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}

First, we try to more formally describe the regime when methods such as bias correction and independent moment estimation can produce 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} with many negative coordinates. We primarily consider bias correction, i.e. Algorithm 7. We will later discuss how the results would change for independent moment estimation (Algorithm 6).

The one-dimensional case: For simplicity let’s fix ζ=1\zeta=1, assume we are in the one-dimensional case and 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} (the averaged clipped gradient) is equal to 𝐠\mathbf{g} for all tt. The corresponding lower bound for 𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(𝝂^t)\mathbf{Var}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}\right) would by a similar derivation be σ21999​B2\frac{\sigma^{2}}{1999B^{2}}. Now, in order for the bias corrected estimate 𝝂^t−ζ2​σ2B2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}-\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}} to be nonnegative with at least, say, probability 1/21/2, a necessary condition is for the standard deviation to be at most a small constant factor times the magnitude of E⁡[𝝂^t−ζ2​σ2B2]=𝐠2E[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}-\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}]=\mathbf{g}^{2}. →B/σ\displaystyle\rightarrow B/\sigma ≳119991/4​1|𝐠|≈0.15⋅1|𝐠|\displaystyle\gtrsim\frac{1}{1999^{1/4}}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{g}|}\approx 0.15\cdot\frac{1}{|\mathbf{g}|}

In the one-dimensional case we might (optimistically) expect 𝐠≈1\mathbf{g}\approx 1, in which case this condition is easily satisfied even for very small batch sizes B≈0.15​σB\approx 0.15\sigma. Even for a more pessimistic 𝐠≈1/B\mathbf{g}\approx 1/\sqrt{B} (what we would get if each individual gradient 𝐠t,j\mathbf{g}_{t,j} was sampled to be 11 or −1-1 w.p. 1/21/2 each), we need B≳0.15​σ\sqrt{B}\gtrsim 0.15\sigma and this condition is still easily satisfied.

The optimistic high-dimensional case: In the mm-dimensional setting, at least 1/21/2 the coordinates of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} (the average of the clipped gradients in round tt) satisfy 𝐠t​(i)≤2​‖𝐠t‖2/m\mathbf{g}_{t}(i)\leq\sqrt{2}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\|_{2}/\sqrt{m}. So even if we optimistically assume ‖𝐠t‖2=1\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\|_{2}=1 (which assumes all examples’ gradients are the same) the sufficient condition for, say, at most 1/41/4 of the coordinates of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} having negative 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} with probability at least 1/21/2 becomes:

B/σ≳0.15​m.B/\sigma\gtrsim 0.15\sqrt{m}. (2)

In other words, as long as the dimension mm is sufficiently small, a method such as bias correction will not produce negative estimates of the second moment frequently. However, if the dimension mm is sufficiently large as a function of the batch size BB, bias correction will frequently produce negative estimates of the second moment, which even with the stability constant can lead to improperly large per-coordinate learning rates (or a large stability constant to regularize these learning rates) and in turn undesirable learning outcomes (we will discuss this further in the next section). As an example, consider setting B=2048,σ=1B=2048,\sigma=1. In this setting, this condition says the dimension should be m≲106m\lesssim 10^{6} to avoid undesirable learning outcomes. Accounting for the fact that some small constants are masked by the approximate inequality, this condition might reasonably hold for research-scale models, but not for slightly larger ones.

The pessimistic high-dimensional case: If GtG_{t}, the per-example gradients in the tt-th batch, were not all the same but instead orthogonal, we would actually get ‖𝐠t‖2≤ζ/B\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\|_{2}\leq\zeta/\sqrt{B}. If we instead plug in ‖𝐠‖2=ζ/B​m\left\|\mathbf{g}\right\|_{2}=\zeta/\sqrt{Bm} for the average coordinate value into (2), we get the condition:

B/σ≳0.15​m.\sqrt{B}/\sigma\gtrsim 0.15\sqrt{m}. (3)

This is now a much more stringent condition. Consider again setting B=2048,σ=1B=2048,\sigma=1, then this condition says the dimension should be m≲2⋅104m\lesssim 2\cdot 10^{4}, far smaller than any modern model size (e.g., even a CNN for MNIST classification has 5⋅1055\cdot 10^{5} parameters).

The high-dimensional case with prefix sums: If using independent moment estimation, we could instead use DP-MF, i.e. noisy prefix sums, to add correlated noise to 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} instead. This might improve the regime in which unbiased estimates of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} avoid frequent negative estimates. For a noisy prefix sum of TT terms ∑t=1Txt\sum_{t=1}^{T}x_{t} with equal sensitivity, DP-MF can achieve variance scaling as O⁡(log3⁡T)O(\log^{3}T) as opposed to O⁡(T)O(T) achieved by independent noise. Due to the decay parameter β2\beta_{2}, 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} is not a prefix sum of equally-weighted terms, but a decaying prefix sum ∑t=1Tβ2T−t​xt\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{2}^{T-t}x_{t}. Determining the variance reduction for decaying prefix sums is a question that to the best of our knowledge has not been addressed by the literature. We can instead optimistically assume DP-MF’s variance is that of just privatizing the “highest-weight” term xTx_{T} in each decaying prefix sum (e.g., in the decay-less case, this corresponds to assuming the variance is O⁡(1)O(1) instead of O⁡(log3⁡T)O(\log^{3}T)). By almost the same derivation, this gives the following lower bound on the variance for e.g. bias-correction for the setting ζ=1,β2=0.999\zeta=1,\beta_{2}=0.999:

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(𝝂^t)≥10−6​(𝐠2​σ2B2+2​σ4B4).\mathbf{Var}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}\right)\geq 10^{-6}\left(\frac{\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{2\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right).

This translates to, for example, the following bound on B/σB/\sigma analogous to e.g. Eq. 2 for the optimistic high-dimensional case:

B/σ≳.032​m.B/\sigma\gtrsim.032\sqrt{m}.

This is a 5×5\times improvement over (3), i.e. a small constant improvement even with an optimistic assumption on the improvement in the variance. In short, this means that using correlated noise does not significantly increase the range of B,σ,mB,\sigma,m for which unbiased estimates of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} avoid bad learning outcomes.

4.4.2 Negative Effects of Negative 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}

Next we explore why having unbiased estimators of 𝝂∗\boldsymbol{\nu}^{*}, or equivalently many negative values in 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, may be harmful for learning. Recall that the default per-coordinate learning rate 1/𝝂1/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\nu}}, which is undefined or imaginary if 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} is non-positive. Hence, bias correction and independent moment estimation effectively use 1/max⁡{𝝂,εs2}1/\sqrt{\max\{\boldsymbol{\nu},\varepsilon_{s}^{2}\}} where εs\varepsilon_{s} is a stability constant instead, to ensure the per-coordinate learning rate is always well-defined and not too large.

What happens if the stability constant εs\varepsilon_{s} is very small? Where 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} is negative, we will end up with a per-coordinate learning rate of 1/εs1/\varepsilon_{s} which is very large. For non-private Adam when the stability constant is the dominating term in 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} and the per-coordinate learning rate is ≈1/εs\approx 1/\varepsilon_{s} this is okay, because this means the gradient in the corresponding coordinate has magnitude at most some constant times εs\varepsilon_{s}, so the resulting update is at most constant in size.

In the presence of noise however, this large per-coordinate learning rate can be much more problematic, at least for the methods we survey: For both bias correction and independent moment estimation, it is possible to have a negative coordinate in 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, but for the corresponding coordinate of the (noisy) gradient to have a magnitude much larger than εs\varepsilon_{s}, either due to the bias correction term or due to the independent noises in independent moment estimation. As a result the update for this coordinate will be very large. If this happens for many coordinates simultaneously, it could potentially cause training to complete diverge. Kalinin et al. [13] propose to clip the final update to avoid this destabilization, but even with this mitigation, the clipped update will have most of its magnitude on coordinates where this destabilization occurred, i.e. the resulting optimizer will be slow to make progress on coordinates which did not destabilize.

We can of course mitigate this by choosing εs\varepsilon_{s} to be larger. However, choosing εs\varepsilon_{s} to be larger will homogenize the values of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} in coordinates where 𝝂∗\boldsymbol{\nu}^{*} is smaller. The bias of the post-processing approach is considered harmful because of this homogenization, so using too large a value of εs\varepsilon_{s} defeats the point of using an unbiased estimator of 𝝂∗\boldsymbol{\nu}^{*} in the first place.

In Section 4.4.1 we showed DP-Adam with bias correction the standard deviation of 𝝂i\boldsymbol{\nu}_{i} is at least a constant times ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}, the bias of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} in DP-Adam via post-processing. So if we are in a regime where a constant fraction of coordinates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} have magnitude at most ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}, i.e. we are in a regime where training is likely to destabilize for small εs\varepsilon_{s}, then we need to set εs2\varepsilon_{s}^{2} to be about as large as the bias correction term ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}} to ensure that the magnitude of the update in any coordinate is at most a constant. But if we set εs2\varepsilon_{s}^{2} to be as large as the bias correction term, we effectively add the bias correction term back to the smallest coordinates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}, undoing the benefits of bias correction. In particular, these are the coordinates where the gradient signal is sparsest or smallest, and where we arguably could benefit the most from adaptive optimization.

For independent moment estimation the high-level story is similar, although the negative values in 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} now come from adding negative noise to 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} rather than from subtracting a bias correction. This introduces an additional adverse effect, where the per-coordinate learning rate of a coordinate could be 1/εs1/\varepsilon_{s}, but the gradient could have a large noise value added to it, and we will hence take a large noise update on this coordinate. Put another way, DP-Adam via post-processing (or with bias correction) has a self-regularization behavior where if large noise is added to one coordinate of the gradient, the corresponding coordinate of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} will be large, hence the per-coordinate learning rate will be small and we avoid taking a large noisy update in that coordinate. The decoupling of noises in independent moment estimation prevents this self-regularization.

In short, in the regime where many of 𝝂∗\boldsymbol{\nu}^{*}’s coordinates are smaller than the bias ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}, DP-Adam with bias correction or independent moment estimation is forced to either destabilize, clip the updates and progress slowly on coordinates where 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} is large, or use a large stability constant that effectively undoes the bias correction. We emphasize that these behaviors may not be problematic if most coordinates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} are sufficiently large, which e.g. is more likely to happen in low-dimensional settings. Hence our claim is not that bias correction or independent moment estimation universally introduce adverse effects to private adaptive optimizers, just that there are some parameter regimes where they do.

Conclusions: To summarize this section, one can think of there being two regimes in terms of m,B,σm,B,\sigma. One regime is where Eq. 2 (or Eq. 3, if being pessimistic) holds, and methods such as bias correction avoid undesirable learning outcomes (and as we will demonstrate later, may even be strongly preferable to other methods). The second regime is where Eq. 2 fails to hold, and bias correction may actually impede learning performance.

Based on these observations, we caution against the use of DP variants of Adam which preserve unbiasedness of the second moment estimate in high-dimensional regimes, and conclusions from experiments using these variants in low-dimensional settings should not be expected to hold in higher-dimensional settings.

4.5 Scale-Then-Privatize and Prefix Sums

We now consider the interplay between scale-then-privatize and DP-MF. The main goal of DP-MF is to cancel out noise across different iterations. When the underlying optimizer is SGD, the learning rate remains constant across iterations so the total noise added to the sum of the first tt optimizer updates is a prefix sum proportional to ∑j=1t(𝐂−1​𝐳)j\sum_{j=1}^{t}({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}. Hence, the line of work on DP-MF proposes to choose 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} that minimizes the RMSE, i.e. average of the variances of prefix sums {∑j=1t(𝐂−1​𝐳)j}t\{\sum_{j=1}^{t}({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}\}_{t}. This is equivalent to optimizing the tradeoff between noise cancellation and increased sensitivity, and can be done entirely offline, i.e. before starting training.

Before understanding how to optimize 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} for Adam, as an intermediate we can understand SGD with momentum parameter β1\beta_{1}. SGD with momentum initializes a momentum μ0\mu_{0}, and uses the update μt=β1​μt−1+𝐠t\mu_{t}=\beta_{1}\mu_{t-1}+\mathbf{g}_{t}, 𝜽t=𝜽t−1−η​μt\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t-1}-\eta\mu_{t}. Without clipping or noise, the iterates 𝜽t+1\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} of SGD with momentum β1\beta_{1} can be expressed as a linear combination of the gradients 𝐠1,…,𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{g}_{t}, namely

𝜽t+1=𝜽0+∑j=1t(∑k=0t−jβ1k)​𝐠j,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-j}\beta_{1}^{k}\right)\mathbf{g}_{j},

and hence the total noise in 𝜽t+1\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} in SGD with momentum using DP-MF to add noise is

∑j=1t(∑k=0t−jβ1k)​(𝐂−1​𝐳)i\sum_{j=1}^{t}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-j}\beta_{1}^{k}\right)({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{i}

and we could again choose 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} that minimizes the average variance of the noises {∑j=1t(∑k=0t−jβ1k)​(𝐂−1​𝐳)i}\{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-j}\beta_{1}^{k}\right)({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{i}\} before starting optimization. However, Choquette-Choo et al. [6] observe optimizing for this objective instead of the momentum-less objective has minimal to no benefit for training models; that is, we can use 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} optimized for SGD without momentum, even for SGD with momentum, and empirically this is about as good.

Now, we consider how to privatize DP-Adam. The main challenge in contrast with SGD is that in Algorithm 5 (DP-Adam via post-processing) and most other variants we’ve discussed, the noise added to the sum of the optimizer updates is (setting the stability parameter εs=0\varepsilon_{s}=0) proportional to ∑j=1t∑k=jtβ1t−k1−β1t​(𝐂−1​𝐳)j𝝂^k\sum_{j=1}^{t}\sum_{k=j}^{t}\frac{\beta_{1}^{t-k}}{1-\beta_{1}^{t}}\frac{({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{k}}}; note that up to the scaling by 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} and normalization of the momentum 11−β1t\frac{1}{1-\beta_{1}^{t}}, this retrieves SGD with momentum β1\beta_{1}. So if we assume that, similarly to SGD, it suffices in practice to optimize for the momentum-less objective, then we want to minimize the average variance of the noises added to prefix sums {∑j=1t(𝐂−1​𝐳)j𝝂^j}\{\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}}}\}.

The main challenge is that even with this simplifying assumption, the term 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} is determined in an online manner, and is not known prior to beginning optimization. That is, unlike SGD, we cannot optimize the matrix 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} in an offline manner because the coefficient 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} in the prefix sum only appears during training. Furthermore, for SGD the noise being added to each coordinate is the same, i.e. we can optimize a single 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} and use it to noise all coordinates simultaneously. In contrast, for DP-Adam even if 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} was given offline, we would want to apply different choices of noise correlation 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} to different coordinates, but e.g. DP composition theorems don’t give us a straightforward way to do this. We argue that scale-then-privatize mitigates both these issues. For scale-then-privatize (Algorithm 8) we instead want to minimize the variance of:

∑j=1t(𝐂−1​𝐳)j/𝐬j𝝂^j=∑j=1t(𝐂−1​𝐳)j𝝂^j/𝝂^j−1.\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}/\mathbf{s}_{j}}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}}}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{j}}{\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}/\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j-1}}}.

Recall that

𝝂^t=β2−β2t1−β2t​𝝂^t−1+1−β21−β2t​(𝐠+ζB​(𝐂−1​𝐳)t)2,\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}=\frac{\beta_{2}-\beta_{2}^{t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\left(\mathbf{g}+\frac{\zeta}{B}({{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}}\mathbf{z})_{t}\right)^{2},

and as tt increases β2−β2t1−β2t\frac{\beta_{2}-\beta_{2}^{t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}} approaches β2\beta_{2} which is usually set to a constant close to 1 like .999.999 in practice. This means that without momentum, even if the squared gradients wildly differ in consecutive iterations, the scaling 𝝂^j/𝝂^j−1\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}/\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j-1}} approaches nearly 𝟏\boldsymbol{1}. This mitigates both of the aforementioned issues: First, for optimizing 𝐂\mathbf{C} for DP-Adam with scale-then-privatize, if we treat 𝝂^j/𝝂^j−1=1\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}/\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j-1}}=1 we retrieve an objective that can be optimized offline. Furthermore, this objective is nearly the same as that of DP-SGD with momentum, i.e. we can use the same methods to choose 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} as for DP-SGD and be reasonably confident in the resulting choice of 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} having good utility). Second, if 𝝂^j/𝝂^j−1≈1\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}/\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j-1}}\approx 1 then the objective is roughly the same for all coordinates, i.e. we can optimize a single 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} and use it to noise all coordinates at a minimal loss in utility.

5 Empirical Comparisons

In this section we compare different variants of DP-Adam, with and without DP-MF, in different settings.

5.1 1-Dimensional Logistic Regression

We first consider AdaGrad (Algorithm 3) in the 1-dimensional setting. We consider a synthetic sparse logistic regression setup. We generate data inputs (x,y)(x,y) where x∼N⁡(0,1),y∼B​e​r​n​(11+e−x)x\sim N(0,1),y\sim Bern(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}). Given an input (x,y)(x,y), y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} and model 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} the loss is ℓ⁡(𝜽,(x,y))=y​log⁡(1p)+(1−y)​log⁡(11−p)\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};(x,y))=y\log\left(\frac{1}{p}\right)+(1-y)\log\left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right) where p=11+e−𝜽​xp=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\boldsymbol{\theta}x}}; the ground truth corresponds to 𝜽=1\boldsymbol{\theta}=1. We consider a sparse setting where for 90%90\% of the training data we set x=0x=0, i.e. the gradient ∇𝜽ℓ​(𝜽,(x;y))\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};(x;y)) is 00. In this setting, using AdaGrad (whose learning rate decays with the number of non-zero samples seen so far, instead of the number of samples seen so far) is preferable to SGD with decaying learning rate. We generate 1000 training samples and do a single epoch with batch size 1, and use clip norm ζ=1.0\zeta=1.0 and noise multiplier σ=0.1\sigma=0.1; in other words, we have B/σ=10B/\sigma=10 which is a relatively small signal-to-noise ratio compared to modern large-scale DP training pipelnies. We tune the base learning rate η\eta.

We compare four approaches, using DP-MF optimized for single-epoch training without any constraint on the strategy matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C}:

    AdaGrad without any noise.

  • •

    DP AdaGrad via post-processing, i.e. we privatize the gradients and then use AdaGrad as a black-box.

  • •

    DP AdaGrad via independent moment estimation, i.e. we separately noise the gradient 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} and its square 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2}, and use the noisy 𝐠t2\mathbf{g}_{t}^{2} to update the noisy estimate 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} of ∑j=1t𝐠j2\sum_{j=1}^{t}\mathbf{g}_{j}^{2}. Since this estimate can be negative with noise, we use a learning rate of η/max⁡{1,𝝂^}\eta/\max\{1,\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\} instead of η/𝝂^\eta/\sqrt{\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}} in round tt. By default we use σ=0.1⋅2\sigma=0.1\cdot\sqrt{2}, but we also try independent moment estimation “for free,” i.e. using σ=0.1\sigma=0.1.

In Fig. 2 we compare the test loss of the final model on 10,00010,000 samples (not sparsified) of each approach. For the noisy variants, we report the average of 30 trials. We see that despite the relatively small value of B/σB/\sigma, and even if independent moment estimation incurs extra noise, independent moment estimation achieves better performance than post-processing. While our later experiments will show that independent moment estimation is uncompetitive in the high-dimensional regime (matching the intuition built in Section 4), this makeshift experiment provides evidence that in the low-dimensional regime it is a well-performing variant.

5.2 High-Dimensional Transformer Training

We next focus on a transformer training setup. We fine-tune a pretrained TinyBERT model (approximately 4.44.4 million trainable parameters) on the masked token prediction task as defined in [9] for the arXiv dataset. The arXiv dataset consists of ≈\approx1.9 million papers. We use each paper’s abstract, truncated to 512 tokens, as a text example for training. We randomly split the dataset into a train/test/validation split of ≈\approx 1.7/0.1/0.1 million examples each. We use 2000 iterations of training with a batch size of 2048 (such that each example participates at most 33 times). We fix the clip norm of 1.01.0 (when not using scale-then-privatize), which we found to be effective across all settings. As we are primarily concerned with comparing different variants of adaptive optimizers, which for a given DP guarantee will all use the same distribution of noise 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}, we fix a noise multiplier across all experiments and ignore its mapping to a specific DP guarantee (including e.g. accounting for amplification, group sizes, etc.). For correlated noise, we use DP-BandMF of [7] and noise multiplier of 11 (with b=b=128 bands for efficiency). We also use independent noise with noise multiplier of ≈.134\approx.134 and 11, such that the RMSE of prefix sums (as defined in e.g., [6]) and the example-level ε\varepsilon respectively are the same for independent noise and correlated noise. We are primarily concerned about the effects of noise on DP-Adam and less concerned about the specific ε\varepsilon the noise corresponds to, so we do not worry about amplification when computing ε\varepsilon for simplicity, i.e. our results on DP-MF vs DP-SGD do not necessarily indicate one or the other is better when combined with adaptive optimizers in settings where amplification is available.

In Fig. 3 we compare the average test loss across 30 trials of the following variants of DP-Adam:

  • •

    Post-processing (Algorithm 5). We tune the learning rate only.

  • •

    Independent moment estimation (Algorithm 6). We tune the learning rate and the stability constant εs\varepsilon_{s}.

  • •

    Bias correction (Algorithm 7). We tune the learning rate and the stability constant εs\varepsilon_{s}.

  • •

    Scale-then-privatize (Algorithm 8). We tune the learning rate, stability constant used for clipping εs1\varepsilon_{s_{1}}, and re-tune the clip norm since we are no longer clipping in the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm.

  • •

    Noiseless preconditioner (a variant of Algorithm 9). As previously discussed, we add noise to the gradients but use the value of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} computed using the noiseless gradients. This is a non-private baseline purely for the sake of understanding the value of getting better estimates of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu}. We try the noiseless preconditioner with and without scale-then-privatize.

We also validate the necessity of using Adam for this task by comparing to SGD (with a tuned momentum parameter), both with and without noise.

Our main observation is that independent moment estimation consistently does worse than the baseline DP-Adam via post-processing, and bias correction slightly improves on this baseline in a very high-epsilon setting but otherwise does worse. In contrast, scale-then-privatize consistently improves on the post-processing approach. This is in contrast with the 1-dimensional setting, i.e., the performance of independent moment estimation and bias correction degrades in higher dimensions, matching the intuition developed in Section 4.

In addition to scale-then-privatize outperforming the other approaches, our noiseless preconditioner baselines offer some support for our theoretical observations. Without scale-then-privatize, switching to a noiseless preconditioner in DP-Adam leads to roughly the same test loss. This suggests that even if we can retrieve the ability of Adam to learn the geometry of the noiseless of the gradients, the benefits of this are negated by the fact that this geometry is a mismatch with the geometry of the noisy gradients, as demonstrated with the running example of Section 4.1. In contrast, with scale-then-privatize, using a noiseless preconditioner improves utility, slightly for DP-SGD in the low-noise setting and significantly for DP-MF. This demonstrates that when the geometry of the noiseless and noisy gradients are similar (as we demonstrated in Section 4.3.2), better estimates of the preconditioner are indeed helpful.

We can further validate the theoretical intuition of Section 4.4.1 by demonstrating that bias correction retrieves many negative coordinates in this setting. In Fig. 4 we plot the fraction of coordinates of 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} which are negative after bias correction, when using DP-Adam with independent noise and σ≈0.134\sigma\approx 0.134. We see that anywhere from 45%45\% to 50%50\% of coordinates are negative in most rounds of training. In Fig. 5 we also check the norm of the averaged clipped gradients 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t}, divided by the clip norm (in our experiments, just 1.01.0) for DP-Adam via post-processing with independent noise and σ≈.134\sigma\approx.134. A value of 1.0 corresponds to the “optimistic” setting in Section 4.4.1, and a value of 1/B=1/2048≈.0221/\sqrt{B}=1/\sqrt{2048}\approx.022 corresponds to the “pessimistic” setting. The average value across all rounds is roughly 0.270.27, suggesting we are closer to the optimistic regime, i.e. most pairs of gradients have a reasonably high dot product with each other. The fact that the fraction of negative coordinates in Fig. 4 is large in spite of this can be explained by the magnitudes of the gradients across different coordinates. The analysis in Section 4.4.1 is optimistic in that it gives sufficient lower bounds for BB (as a function of σ,m\sigma,m) assuming the magnitudes of gradients (and hence the values of 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}) are roughly uniform across the coordinates. In Fig. 6 we plot the values of 𝝂\boldsymbol{\nu} arrived at by non-private Adam and compare them to the bias correction term ζ2​σ2B2\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}, and we see most coordinates fall below the bias correction term in magnitude. Furthermore, for bias correction and independent moment estimation, in all settings the best value of the stability constant εs\varepsilon_{s} was 10−410^{-4}, which corresponds to imposing a floor on the preconditioner values of 10−810^{-8}. As we can see in Fig. 6 this exceeds the magnitude of the bias correction; this validates the intuition from Section 4.4.1 that in order to mitigate the negative effects of bias correction or independent moment estimation we need to use a stability constant sufficiently large to effectively re-introduce the bias of DP-Adam via post-processing for small coordinates of ν^\hat{\nu}.

Finally, we note that unlike what was observed in past works for DP-SGD, for DP-Adam the RMSE of the noising mechanism is not a good predictor of learning performance, in spite of the observations made in Section 4.5. This matches an observation made in [17]. It is an interesting future direction to explore what objectives for optimizing the choice of 𝐂−1{{\mathbf{C}}^{-1}} are best for adaptive optimizers.

Appendix A Bias Correction for DP-MF

We focus on the one-dimensional case, i.e. the gradients are scalars, as in the higher-dimensional case the bias is just the bias in the one-dimensional case times 𝟏\boldsymbol{1}. For DP-Adam with DP-MF the second moment estimate in iteration tt is (given decay parameter β<1\beta<1):

𝝂^t=1−β21−β2t⋅∑i=1t𝐠i2⋅β2i−1.\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}=\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbf{g}_{i}^{2}\cdot\beta_{2}^{i-1}.

Let 𝐃⁡(β2,t)\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t) be the diagonal matrix 1−β21−β2t⋅diag⁡(β2t−1,β2t−2,…,β2,1)\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\cdot\diag(\beta_{2}^{t-1},\beta_{2}^{t-2},\ldots,\beta_{2},1). Then 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} be written as 𝐠:t⊤𝐃(β2,t)𝐠:t\mathbf{g}_{:t}^{\top}\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t)\mathbf{g}_{:t}, where 𝐠:t=(𝐠1,𝐠2,…,𝐠t)\mathbf{g}_{:t}=(\mathbf{g}_{1},\mathbf{g}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{g}_{t}). Defining 𝐳:t\mathbf{z}_{:t} analogously, the bias is then:

𝔼[(𝐠:t+(𝐂:t,:t−1)𝐳:t)⊤𝐃(β2,t)(𝐠:t+(𝐂:t,:t−1)𝐳:t)]−𝐠:t⊤𝐃(β2,t)𝐠:t\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{g}_{:t}+(\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t})\mathbf{z}_{:t})^{\top}\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t)(\mathbf{g}_{:t}+(\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t})\mathbf{z}_{:t})]-\mathbf{g}_{:t}^{\top}\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t)\mathbf{g}_{:t} =𝔼[𝐳:t⊤(𝐂:t,:t−1)⊤𝐃(β2,t)(𝐂:t,:t−1)𝐳:t]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}_{:t}^{\top}(\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t})^{\top}\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t)(\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t})\mathbf{z}_{:t}]
=Tr((𝐂:t,:t−1)⊤𝐃(β2,t)(𝐂:t,:t−1))⋅ζ2​σ2B2.\displaystyle=\Tr((\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t})^{\top}\mathbf{D}(\beta_{2},t)(\mathbf{C}^{-1}_{:t,:t}))\cdot\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}.

We can also write this as a recursive formula. If the bias correction is bib_{i} in iteration tt, b0=0b_{0}=0, we have:

bt+1=β2−β2t+11−β2t+1​bi+β2⋅1−β21−β2t+1​((𝐂−1)⊤​𝐂−1)t+1,t+1⋅ζ2​σ2B2.b_{t+1}=\frac{\beta_{2}-\beta_{2}^{t+1}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t+1}}b_{i}+\beta_{2}\cdot\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t+1}}((\mathbf{C}^{-1})^{\top}\mathbf{C}^{-1})_{t+1,t+1}\cdot\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}.

𝝂^t\displaystyle\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} =𝝂t/(1−β2t)=(β2​𝝂t−1+(1−β2)​𝐠~t2)/(1−β2t)=β2−β2t1−β2t​𝝂^t−1+1−β21−β2t​𝐠~t2\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t}/\left(1-\beta_{2}^{t}\right)=\left(\beta_{2}\boldsymbol{\nu}_{t-1}+\left(1-\beta_{2}\right)\widetilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t}^{2}\right)/\left(1-\beta_{2}^{t}\right)=\frac{\beta_{2}-\beta_{2}^{t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\widetilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t}^{2}

Appendix C Generalized Analysis from Section 4.4.1

Similarly to Eq. 1, we have:

𝝂^1=(𝐠+ζB​𝐳1)2,𝝂^t=β2−β2t1−β2t​𝝂^t−1+1−β21−β2t​(𝐠+ζB​𝐳t)2.\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{1}=\left(\mathbf{g}+\frac{\zeta}{B}\mathbf{z}_{1}\right)^{2},\qquad\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}=\frac{\beta_{2}-\beta_{2}^{t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t-1}+\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\left(\mathbf{g}+\frac{\zeta}{B}\mathbf{z}_{t}\right)^{2}.

Unrolling the recursion we have:

𝝂^t=∑j=1t(1−β2)​β2t−j1−β2t​(𝐠+ζB​𝐳j)2=𝝂^t∗+∑j=1t(1−β2)​β2t−j1−β2t​(ζB​𝐠𝐳j+ζ2B2​𝐳j2).\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{(1-\beta_{2})\beta_{2}^{t-j}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\left(\mathbf{g}+\frac{\zeta}{B}\mathbf{z}_{j}\right)^{2}=\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}^{*}+\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{(1-\beta_{2})\beta_{2}^{t-j}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\left(\frac{\zeta}{B}\mathbf{g}\mathbf{z}_{j}+\frac{\zeta^{2}}{B^{2}}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{2}\right).

Since 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} is a Gaussian and thus symmetric, 𝐂𝐨𝐯⁡(𝐳t,𝐳t2)=0\mathbf{Cov}\left(\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{z}_{t}^{2}\right)=0. So the variance of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} is

=(1−β21−β2t)2​∑j=1tβ22​(t−j)​(ζ2​𝐠2B2​𝐕𝐚𝐫​(𝐳j)+ζ4B4​𝐕𝐚𝐫​(𝐳j2))\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\right)^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{t}\beta_{2}^{2(t-j)}\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}}{B^{2}}\mathbf{Var}\left(\mathbf{z}_{j}\right)+\frac{\zeta^{4}}{B^{4}}\mathbf{Var}\left(\mathbf{z}_{j}^{2}\right)\right)

=(ζ2​𝐠2​σ2B2+2​ζ4​σ4B4)​(1−β21−β2t)2​1−β22​t1−β22\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{2\zeta^{4}\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right)\left(\frac{1-\beta_{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}\right)^{2}\frac{1-\beta_{2}^{2t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}
=(ζ2​𝐠2​σ2B2+2​ζ4​σ4B4)​(1−β2)21−β22⋅1−β22​t(1−β2t)2\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{2\zeta^{4}\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right)\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\cdot\frac{1-\beta_{2}^{2t}}{(1-\beta_{2}^{t})^{2}}
≥(ζ2​𝐠2​σ2B2+2​ζ4​σ4B4)​(1−β2)21−β22\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{2\zeta^{4}\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right)\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}

Now, in order for the bias corrected estimate 𝝂^t−ζ2​σ2B2\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}-\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}} to be non-negative with at least, say, probability 1/21/2, a necessary condition is for the standard deviation to be within a constant factor of the magnitude of E⁡[𝝂^t−ζ2​σ2B2]=𝐠2E[\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}-\frac{\zeta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}]=\mathbf{g}^{2}. Rearranging, we get:

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(𝝂^t)\displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbf{Var}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}\right)} ≲𝐠2\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbf{g}^{2}
