→(ζ2​𝐠2​σ2B2+ζ4​σ4B4)​(1−β2)21−β22\displaystyle\rightarrow\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{\zeta^{4}\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right)\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}} ≲𝐠4\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbf{g}^{4}
→B/σ\displaystyle\rightarrow B/\sigma ≳((1−β2)21−β22)1/4​ζ|𝐠|.\displaystyle\gtrsim\left(\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/4}\frac{\zeta}{|\mathbf{g}|}.

In the one-dimensional case, if the clip norm ζ\zeta is chosen appropriately we might (optimistically) expect 𝐠≈ζ\mathbf{g}\approx\zeta, in which case this condition is easily satisfied even for small batch sizes (as a function of σ\sigma). Even for a more pessimistic 𝐠≈ζ/B\mathbf{g}\approx\zeta/\sqrt{B} (what we would get if 𝐠\mathbf{g} was sampled to be ζ\zeta or −ζ-\zeta w.p. 1/21/2 each), this condition is still easily satisfied.

The optimistic high-dimensional case: In the mm-dimensional setting, at least 1/21/2 the coordinates of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} (the average of the clipped gradients in round tt) satisfy 𝐠t​(i)≤2​‖𝐠t‖2/m\mathbf{g}_{t}(i)\leq\sqrt{2}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\|_{2}/\sqrt{m}. So even if we optimistically assume ‖𝐠t‖2=ζ\left\|\mathbf{g}_{t}\right\|_{2}=\zeta (which assumes all examples gradients are the same) the sufficient condition for, say, at most 1/41/4 of the coordinates of 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} having negative 𝝂^\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}} with probability 1/21/2 becomes:

B/σ≳((1−β2)21−β22)1/4​m.B/\sigma\gtrsim\left(\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/4}\sqrt{m}. (6)

In other words, as long as the dimension mm is sufficiently small, a method such as bias correction will not produce negative estimates of the second moment frequently. However, if the dimension mm is sufficiently large as a function of the batch size BB, bias correction will frequently produce negative estimates of the second moment, which even with the stability constant can lead to improperly large per-coordinate learning rates (or a large stability constant to regularize these learning rates) and in turn undesirable learning outcomes (we will discuss this further in the next section). As an example, consider e.g. B=2048,σ=1,β2=.999B=2048,\sigma=1,\beta_{2}=.999, this condition says the dimension should be at most roughly m≲106m\lesssim 10^{6} to avoid undesirable learning outcomes. Accounting for the fact that some small constants are masked by the approximate inequality, this condition might reasonably hold for research-scale models, but not for slightly larger ones.

The pessimistic high-dimensional case: If the per-example gradients in a batch were not all the same, but instead orthogonal, we would actually get ‖𝐠‖2≤ζ/B\left\|\mathbf{g}\right\|_{2}\leq\zeta/\sqrt{B}. If we instead plug in |𝐠|=ζ/B​m|\mathbf{g}|=\zeta/\sqrt{Bm} for the average coordinate value into (6), we get the condition:

B/σ≳((1−β2)21−β22)1/4​m.\sqrt{B}/\sigma\gtrsim\left(\frac{(1-\beta_{2})^{2}}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/4}\sqrt{m}. (7)

This is now a much more stringent condition. Consider e.g. B=2048,σ=1,β2=.999B=2048,\sigma=1,\beta_{2}=.999, this condition says the dimension should be at most roughly m≲2⋅104m\lesssim 2\cdot 10^{4}, far smaller than any modern model size (e.g., even a CNN for MNIST classification has 5⋅1055\cdot 10^{5} parameters).

The high-dimensional case with prefix sums: If using independent moment estimation, we could instead use DP-MF, i.e. noisy prefix sums, to add correlated noise to 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} instead. This might improve the regime in which unbiased estimates of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} avoid frequent negative estimates. For a noisy prefix sum of TT terms ∑t=1Txt\sum_{t=1}^{T}x_{t} with equal sensitivity, DP-MF can achieve variance scaling as O⁡(log3⁡T)O(\log^{3}T) as opposed to O⁡(T)O(T) achieved by independent noise. Due to the decay parameter β2\beta_{2}, 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} is not a prefix sum of equally-weighted terms, but a decaying prefix sum ∑t=1Tβ2T−i​xt\sum_{t=1}^{T}\beta_{2}^{T-i}x_{t}. Determining the variance reduction for decaying prefix sums is a question that to the best of our knowledge has not been addressed by the literature. We can instead optimistically assume DP-MF’s variance is that of just privatizing the “highest-weight” term xTx_{T} in each decaying prefix sum (e.g., in the decay-less case, this corresponds to assuming the variance is O⁡(1)O(1) instead of O⁡(log3⁡T)O(\log^{3}T)). By almost the same derivation, this gives the following lower bound on the variance for e.g. bias-correction:

𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(𝝂^t)≥(ζ2​𝐠2​σ2B2+2​ζ4​σ4B4)​(1−β2)2.\mathbf{Var}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t}\right)\geq\left(\frac{\zeta^{2}\mathbf{g}^{2}\sigma^{2}}{B^{2}}+\frac{2\zeta^{4}\sigma^{4}}{B^{4}}\right)(1-\beta_{2})^{2}.

In turn, using correlated noise improves the lower bound on B/σB/\sigma by a factor of (11−β22)1/4\left(\frac{1}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/4}. For example, we get the following bound on B/σB/\sigma analogous to e.g. Eq. 6:

B/σ≳(1−β2)1/2​m.B/\sigma\gtrsim(1-\beta_{2})^{1/2}\sqrt{m}.

For the standard β2=.999\beta_{2}=.999, we have (11−β22)1/4≈4.73\left(\frac{1}{1-\beta_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/4}\approx 4.73, i.e. a small constant improvement even with an optimistic assumption on the improvement in the variance. In short, this means that using correlated noise does not significantly increase the range of B,σ,mB,\sigma,m for which unbiased estimates of 𝝂^t\hat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{t} avoid bad learning outcomes.
